citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.2(7)
title: Definition of 'deficiency' in service
content: Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines 'deficiency' as a defect or shortcoming in the quality of service which is required to be maintained by or under any law, or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise. Section 2(8) extends this to 'deficiency in service', meaning any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality of the service which is required to be maintained by or under any law, or which has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise. Together these sections are the foundation of a medical negligence complaint: a plaintiff must show that the service provided by the hospital or practitioner fell below the standard required by law, by contract, or by the profession's own norms.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.2(11)
title: Definition of 'service' — includes medical treatment
content: Section 2(11) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines 'service' as service of any description made available to potential users and includes banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, board or lodging, housing construction, entertainment, amusement, news or information, but does not include services which are free of charge, or provided by the central government, a state government or a local authority. The definition is open-ended and non-exhaustive. It is the principal statutory hook for treating medical treatment by a hospital or doctor as a 'service' renderable for profit, and therefore a consumer dispute within the jurisdiction of the consumer commissions.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.2(42)
title: Definition of 'service provider'
content: Section 2(42) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines 'service provider' as a person who provides any service in relation to any goods or under a contract of service, personal or otherwise. Critically, the definition includes both the person who provides the service directly and a person who holds himself out as being engaged in the provision of services, including a person who holds himself out as a person who provides or supplies services. This is why both an individual doctor and a corporate hospital can be jointly sued in the same consumer complaint where the doctor is an employee, consultant or visiting specialist of the hospital.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.34
title: Jurisdiction of District Commission — claims up to fifty lakh rupees
content: Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 vests the District Commission with jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees. This threshold has remained unchanged from the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The District Commission is the first adjudicatory authority for a consumer dispute and is ordinarily located at the district headquarters of the State where the opposite party resides or carries on business. A claimant whose total relief exceeds fifty lakh rupees must approach the State Commission, and one exceeding two crore rupees must approach the National Commission.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.35
title: Redressal of complaints — inherent power to pass interim and final orders
content: Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 sets out the redressal of complaints. Sub-section (2) provides that where the facts of the case admit of clear-cut issues, the Commission may decide them on the basis of pleadings alone. Sub-section (3) permits summary determination where the defendant does not contest the complaint or denies the allegations but leaves the evidence to the Commission. Sub-section (4) confers the wide power to pass interim orders to preserve and protect the parties' interests, including orders for inspection of records, appointment of experts and preservation of evidence. Sub-section (5) allows the Commission to pass orders for the payment of compensation where the complaint is proved.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.38
title: General provisions applicable to consumer dispute redressal commissions
content: Section 38 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 lays down the general provisions applicable to redressal commissions. Section 38(1) enables a complainant to withdraw the complaint or to settle the dispute at any time, subject to the requirement that the terms of settlement are not harsh or unjust to the complainants. Section 38(2) deals with the period within which a complaint shall be decided where the complaint is not satisfied earlier, ordinarily within ninety days. Section 38(5) provides that where the complaint is dismissed, the Commission shall record reasons for its order. These provisions govern the conduct and timelines of a medical negligence complaint.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.46
title: Jurisdiction of State Commission — claims above fifty lakh up to two crore rupees
content: Section 46 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 vests the State Commission with jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds fifty lakh rupees but does not exceed two crore rupees. Where a complaint exceeds the pecuniary limit of the forum in which it is filed, the Commission may, in the absence of a sufficient cause, either return the complaint for filing in the appropriate forum or, in the case of a complaint involving a value not exceeding ten lakh rupees, admit it and decide the matter. Where the excess claim does not exceed a further ten lakh rupees the Commission may similarly admit the matter in certain circumstances.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.47
title: Jurisdiction of National Commission — claims exceeding two crore rupees
content: Section 47 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 vests the National Commission with jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds two crore rupees. The National Commission also has concurrent jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the Central Government has been directed to be joined as a respondent under section 71, and where the complaint involves a question of law of general importance that requires interpretation of law on which a State Commission or the High Court has already expressed an opinion.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.62
title: Appeal against order of District Commission
content: Section 62 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides that a complainant as well as the opposite party may appeal against the order of the District Commission. Sub-section (2) requires that a memorandum of appeal be prepared by the appellant and presented within thirty days of the date of the order, with a copy of the order appended, and that it be accompanied by a fee as prescribed by the Central Government. Section 62(4) further provides that the appeal shall be disposed of within ninety days of the date of presentation. Appeals lie from the State Commission to the National Commission under section 47.

citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.69
title: Two-year limitation period for consumer complaints
content: Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides that a complaint under the Act shall be admitted only if the complaint is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. Sub-section (2) provides an exception where the complainant satisfies the Commission that he had sufficient cause for not being able to file the complaint within the stipulated period, in which case the Commission may admit the complaint if satisfied that the delay was justified and the facts of the case merit adjudication. This two-year period is the operative limitation for a medical negligence complaint, and it differs from the three-year period under section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 that applies to ordinary civil suits for compensation.

citation: Limitation Act, 1963, s.3
title: Three-year limitation for ordinary suits — contrast with the Consumer Act
content: Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides that every suit instituted in respect of any matter which the competent court is barred from entertaining, and every suit for compensation for a wrong, must be instituted within three years from the date on which the cause of action arises. A medical negligence claim pursued in a civil suit rather than before a consumer commission therefore carries a three-year limitation period, whereas a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 carries two years under section 69 of that Act. Choosing the forum changes the limitation clock, and in several cases the two-year period expires before the three-year one.

citation: Limitation Act, 1963, s.27
title: Fresh limitation on discovery of fraud or mistake
content: Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides that in the case of a suit for compensation for a wrong or in a suit for the recovery of money where the wrong is not apparent on the face of the suit, the period of limitation begins to run from the date when the wrong or mistake comes to the knowledge of the party against whom the right is claimed. Section 28 similarly addresses suits based on fraud or mistake. This is relevant in medical negligence because the injury may be latent, or the misdiagnosis may only become apparent when a later investigation or second opinion reveals it, and the limitation clock is then treated as starting from that date of knowledge.

citation: Limitation Act, 1963, s.12 and s.14
title: Exclusion of time and exception to section 3
content: Section 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963 excludes from the period of limitation the time during which the party was prevented from instituting the suit by another proceeding properly instituted in a court of competent jurisdiction. Section 14 provides that in computing the period of limitation for any suit, the period during which the plaintiff has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding, whether in a court of competent jurisdiction or one incapable of jurisdiction, against the same party, shall be excluded. These provisions matter in medical negligence litigation where a complaint filed in the wrong forum is challenged on limitation, and where the plaintiff was simultaneously pursuing a criminal case or a writ.

citation: Limitation Act, 1963, s.18
title: Effect of acknowledgment of liability — fresh limitation
content: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides that where, before the expiration of the prescribed period for a suit or application in respect of any property or right, an acknowledgment of liability in respect of such property or right has been made in writing signed by the party against whom the right is claimed, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgment was signed. In medical negligence matters this is significant where the hospital or the treating doctor's written acknowledgement of the incident, or the acceptance of the claim, is relied upon to keep the claim alive. Note that the section is an exception to section 3 and does not by itself apply to complaints governed by section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 without judicial authority.

citation: Limitation Act, 1963, ss.5, 6 and 21
title: Disability of plaintiff — minors, persons of unsound mind and legal capacity
content: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides that a suit for compensation for a wrong suffered by a person who at the time the wrong was committed was a minor, or a person of unsound mind, may be instituted notwithstanding the expiration of the prescribed period, by the person legally entitled to sue. Section 21 defines 'legal disability'. Section 6 provides that in the case of a person suffering from a mental or other physical infirmity capable of being cured, the period of limitation shall begin when the infirmity is cured. Section 28 read with section 29 provides that the disability may be pleaded as ground for setting aside an decree, and if the disability continues for more than six years the party is deemed to have been capable of removing it earlier. These sections are essential in birth injury and delayed-diagnosis cases involving children.

citation: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s.106 (formerly IPC s.304A)
title: Causing death by negligence — criminal liability
content: Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaces section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, provides that a person commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder by causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide by murder. The essential ingredients are a rash or negligent act, attributable to the accused, causing death. The quantum of carelessness required differs from that in a civil negligence claim: criminal liability requires gross negligence showing a total disregard for human life, not merely an error of professional judgement. Both the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 were brought into force in India with effect from 1 July 2024, so section 304A of the Indian Penal Code must be read as section 106 of the Sanhita for acts occurring on or after that date.

citation: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s.9
title: Res judicata — bar of concurrent civil and consumer proceedings
content: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provides that no court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties litigating under the same title in a competent court, and in which such issue was heard and finally decided. Res judicata requires the identity of the parties, the identity of the subject matter, the identity of the cause of action, and a competent court having finally decided the matter. In medical negligence practice this is a live risk where a plaintiff files both a civil suit and a consumer complaint, or where a complaint is withdrawn and refiled, and the cause of action being the same in both proceedings.

citation: Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Art. 22A
title: Professional secrecy of medical records
content: Article 22A of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 73 or section 133 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Sanhita, 2023, no fact of which information is divulged in the course of professional employment is admissible against the person communicating or the person subjected to the communication, unless the communication is made in furtherance of any legal duty or by or to a person having an equal interest in the communication, or unless the person communicating has consented to the admission of the fact. The Supreme Court has held that medical records and films are subject to professional secrecy, but that the patient, or a person acting on the patient's behalf and authorised in writing, may obtain a direction for disclosure under section 33B of the Code of Civil Procedure. Failure of a hospital to disclose records is itself capable of becoming a distinct head of negligence.

citation: Indian Medical Assn. v. V.P. Shanta, (1995) 6 SCC 651
title: Doctor–patient relationship is a 'service' under the Consumer Act
content: The Supreme Court held that the relationship between a patient and a medical practitioner is a consumer relationship, and the service of a physician or hospital is a 'service' within the meaning of the Consumer Protection Act. This removed the principal obstacle that had prevented medical negligence claims from being brought in the consumer fora, an obstacle created when courts had treated the doctor-patient relationship as governed by the general law of tort and had discouraged the use of the consumer forum. The decision means that a patient who has paid for treatment, or who falls within the definition of a 'consumer' by virtue of the service being rendered free but in connection with consideration of hire, can maintain a complaint before the District, State or National Commission.

citation: Spring Meadows Hospital v. Harjol Ahluwalia, (1998) 5 SCC 708
title: Compensation where the patient dies without negligence but after a known negligent act
content: The Supreme Court reversed the High Court's decision and restored compensation to the parents of a patient who had died in the hospital. Although by the time of death the patient had developed unrelated complications, the Court held that where a negligent act by the hospital set the patient on the path of subsequent complications, the hospital could not escape liability merely because a non-negligent cause was the immediate trigger of death. Compensation for loss of a young life, stated the Court, must reflect the value of the life lost, the grief and mental anguish of the parents, and the pecuniary loss to the family, rather than being confined to medical expenses actually incurred.

citation: Achutrao Khedwa v. State of Maharashtra, (1996) 4 SCC 37
title: Elements of negligence and the standard of care in public hospitals
content: The Supreme Court set out the elements that must be established in a negligence claim: (i) a duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff, (ii) breach of that duty by negligence on the part of the defendant, and (iii) consequent damage suffered by the plaintiff as a result of that negligence. The Court emphasised that mere negligence in the conduct of professional work does not by itself constitute a cause of action, because negligence in the absence of damage does not create liability; there must be demonstrable causal connection between the act and the resulting harm. The judgment is also a principal authority for asserting that public hospitals and government medical officers are subject to the same standard of care as private practitioners.

citation: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal, (2004) 10 SCC 139
title: Duty of public hospitals to provide timely treatment
content: The plaintiff patients were being treated at a government hospital in West Bengal and were denied admission, or were turned away, or were not investigated, on the ground that the hospital lacked the necessary facilities. The Supreme Court held that a public hospital rendering service to the poor cannot be permitted to be a byword for callousness, and that the State has a duty to provide basic medical facilities and to treat patients brought to it in an emergency. Government hospitals, it held, are not exempt from the duty of care. The decision is a principal authority where a claim rests on refusal of admission, inordinate delay in treatment, or the absence of emergency equipment or trained staff.

citation: Kusum Sharma and Ors. v. Dr. Asha Khosla and Ors., (2010) 3 SCC 412
title: Consent, standard of care and the physician's duty in emergency situations
content: The plaintiff, a fourteen-year-old girl, suffered a paralytic stroke while under treatment for a stomach complaint. The Court of Appeal had awarded substantial compensation. On appeal to the Supreme Court the compensation was reduced, but the Court clarified several principles. A patient has an absolute right to decide what treatment to accept or refuse, so a failure to disclose the nature and risks of a proposed treatment can constitute negligence and a violation of Article 19(1) of the Constitution. The Court restated that the duty of the medical practitioner is to act with reasonable care and skill, and where the condition of the patient is such that the physician must act quickly, failure to act may itself be negligent.

citation: Savita Garg v. National Hospital and Research Centre, (2004) 6 SCC 314
title: Burden of proof in medical negligence — res ipsa loquitur
content: The plaintiff sued for negligence after a patient, an asthma sufferer, died from an allergic reaction allegedly caused by an injection administered by the hospital. The Supreme Court considered res ipsa loquitur, which permits an inference of negligence to be drawn when the accident is ordinarily the result of the defendant's negligence, the instrumentality causing the harm was under the exclusive control of the defendant, and the plaintiff did not contribute to the event. The Court held that where a patient dies in a hospital without any known cause and without any explanation, the question is whether a reasonable inference of negligence can be drawn. It emphasised that a hospital can rebut such an inference by producing records and evidence of the care actually provided.

citation: Martin F. D'Souza v. Mohd. Ishfaq, (2009) 4 SCC 386
title: Guidelines on instituting medical negligence prosecutions — three expert opinions
content: The Supreme Court laid down guidelines for the prosecution of medical negligence cases under section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, now section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Before a complaint is registered, the police must obtain an opinion from a medical expert from a government or recognised medical college. The accused doctor must be given an opportunity to obtain a counter opinion from another expert, and a third independent expert must then resolve the difference between the two opinions. The complaint proceeds to the Magistrate only if all three experts agree that there is a prima facie case of negligence. A complaint filed in violation of these guidelines is liable to be quashed under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

citation: General Electric Company v. Consumer Education and Research Centre, (1995) 1 SCC 550
title: Indiscriminate and wanton litigation in consumer forums and its condemnation
content: In this judgment, arising from a refusal of the Supreme Court to entertain writ petitions against orders of consumer commissions, the Court expressed deep concern at the filing of frivolous and vexatious complaints in the consumer fora. It observed that indiscriminate and wanton litigations by posters and organisations had damaged the credibility of the consumer redressal mechanism and observed that while the Act was intended to provide a simple and inexpensive remedy, the system should not be allowed to be abused. The judgment is routinely cited by the commissions when dismissing complaints filed without substance, and by appellants arguing that the complaint was not pursued diligently or that the dispute between the parties had been amicably settled.

citation: India Medical Assn. v. Union of India, (1996) 4 SCC 699
title: State power to regulate the medical profession is reasonable and permissible
content: The Supreme Court considered the constitutional validity of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1997's predecessor legislation and the powers of the Central Government and the Medical Council to regulate the medical profession, including the imposition of conditions on registration and the regulation of private practice. The Court held that the regulation of the medical profession, the control on the number and area of practitioners and the maintenance of a register are within the competence of the State, and that the interests of the general public in the health care of the community override the interests of the individual practitioner. The judgment is relevant where liability of a practitioner is founded upon absence of registration or upon professional misconduct.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on the four-fold multiplier
title: Four-fold multiplier applied to base medical expenses
content: Consumer commissions in India have developed a fairly consistent method of quantifying compensation in medical negligence matters. The commission first determines the actual out-of-pocket expenditure incurred by the patient, treating the treatment cost as the base. It then applies a multiplier, conventionally between two and four times the base, to compensate for the mental and physical suffering, the loss of opportunity and the diminution in the quality of life caused by the deficiency in service. Where the negligence has resulted in death, the multiplier is applied to the medical expenses and a separate sum is added for the loss of consortium and the grief of the family. The multiplier is adjusted upwards for grave negligence such as wrong-site surgery or a retained foreign body, and downwards where the patient contributed to the injury.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on loss of earning capacity
title: Loss of earning capacity as a head of compensation
content: Where medical negligence has left a patient with a permanent disability or has reduced the patient's capacity to work, consumer commissions award compensation under the head of loss of earning capacity. The commission ordinarily determines the patient's average monthly or annual income before the injury, applies a disability percentage reflecting the residual functional impairment, and discounts the future earnings to present value over the remaining working life of the patient. Where exact income cannot be proved, the commission may rely on the patient's educational or professional qualifications and the nature of the occupation as a reasonable proxy. Compensation under this head is recoverable in addition to medical expenses and is not subsumed within the general multiplier applied to the treatment cost.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on compensation for mental agony
title: Compensation for mental agony and suffering
content: Every award of compensation in a medical negligence complaint includes a separate head for mental agony, physical pain and the suffering caused to the patient and to the patient's family. In cases resulting in death, the commission awards a sum in respect of the grief and mental anguish of the spouse and the parents, and in respect of the loss of consortium. The quantum is not fixed by any rule and is left to the discretion of the commission, which ordinarily scales it with the gravity of the negligence, the duration of the suffering, the age of the deceased and the manner in which the death or disability occurred. In cases of lingering pain caused by a negligent surgical procedure, this head alone may account for a substantial part of the award.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on partial service and deficiency
title: Compensation where treatment was partial or sub-standard service
content: Where a patient received treatment but the commission finds the service to have been deficient or sub-standard, compensation is not assessed as though no service had been rendered. The commission compares the treatment actually administered with the treatment that ought to have been given, and awards the difference in value together with compensation for the resulting suffering. Where the patient was obliged to undergo a second corrective procedure, the cost of that procedure and the consequent loss are also recoverable. This approach contrasts with a claim for total failure of service, where the whole expenditure is treated as the base for the multiplier together with an additional amount for the resulting hardship.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on award of litigation cost
title: Award of cost of litigation in consumer complaints
content: Consumer commissions habitually award a sum for the cost of the proceedings along with the substantive compensation, reasoning that a consumer who has been compelled to approach the forum for the enforcement of a statutory right should not be penalised for doing so. The award is generally made where the complaint is upheld and the opposite party is substantially unsuccessful. The amount is within the discretion of the commission and is awarded notwithstanding that the consumer may not have engaged a professional advocate, the reasoning being that the statutory forum is intended to be accessible to the consumer. In a medical negligence matter this is usually a minor component of the total award.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on claim escalation and pecuniary jurisdiction
title: Escalation of claim value and pecuniary jurisdiction
content: A frequent practical difficulty in medical negligence matters is that the claim grows as the treatment continues. A complaint filed in the District Commission may begin with a modest claim and later cross the fifty lakh rupee threshold, at which point the forum may object that it has ceased to have pecuniary jurisdiction. Where the claim does not exceed the limit of the next higher forum by a substantial margin, the higher forum may admit and decide the matter, but the cleaner course is to file before the forum competent at the outset. If the forum has already passed a decree, an appeal lies to the next higher commission under section 47 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

citation: Bolam test as applied in India
title: The Bolam test and its Bolitho refinement
content: The Bolam test asks whether the conduct of the defendant conformed to the standard of a reasonably prudent practitioner acting in the same circumstances. Where a body of opinion within the profession holds the practice to be proper, a defendant is not ordinarily found to have been negligent, even if the practice is not the best available. In India the Bolam test was applied for decades, but the Supreme Court in Achutrao Khedwa and subsequently in other decisions restricted its scope: the test cannot be used to justify conduct that is irrational, that no body of competent practitioners would sanction, or that is so divorced from the patient's safety that it is negligent in itself. This refinement, derived from Bolitho, is the practical standard used to determine breach of duty in Indian medical negligence claims today.

citation: Res ipsa loquitur
title: Doctrine of res ipsa loquitur — inferring negligence from the event
content: Res ipsa loquitur, meaning the thing speaks for itself, permits the plaintiff to establish negligence by showing that the harm would not ordinarily occur without negligence, that the instrumentality causing the harm was under the exclusive control of the defendant, and that the plaintiff did not contribute to the event. In medical negligence it is frequently relied upon where a patient suffers an unexpected injury, such as a retained surgical instrument, a wrong-site operation, an unexplained fracture, a nerve injury following an operation, or a death in hospital with no recorded cause. The doctrine shifts the burden onto the defendant to explain the event, and the hospital discharges it by producing contemporaneous records demonstrating the care actually provided.

citation: Vicarious liability of hospitals
title: Hospital liability for acts of consultants and staff
content: A hospital is vicariously liable for the negligence of its employees acting in the course of their employment, and it is generally liable for the acts of visiting consultants and independent practitioners who use its facilities, because the institution exercises control over the premises, the equipment and the treatment. The leading authority is Nilambati Hospital v. V.S. Gopinath. Where a doctor is a full-time employee the hospital may be liable on the ground of respondeat superior alone; where the doctor is an independent consultant, liability arises because the patient entered the hospital and not the doctor's private practice. In most medical negligence claims the plaintiff sues the hospital and the individual practitioner jointly and severally.

citation: Informed consent in medical practice
title: Informed consent — scope, risks and disclosure
content: Informed consent requires the physician to disclose the nature of the proposed treatment, the material risks attaching to it, the alternatives available, and the consequences of declining treatment, in a form the patient can understand. A consent obtained in a printed signature form that does not disclose the material risks does not satisfy this requirement. The Supreme Court in Kusum Sharma treated failure to disclose the risks of a proposed treatment as both a breach of the physician's duty and a violation of the patient's right to decide under Article 19(1) of the Constitution. Consent obtained under duress, obtained from a person with no authority to give it, or obtained for a different procedure than the one performed, is not a defence to a negligence claim.

citation: Burden of proof in medical negligence claims
title: Who must prove negligence
content: In an ordinary civil claim the burden of proving negligence lies on the plaintiff, and in a consumer complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 the burden lies on the complainant who must produce evidence of service deficiency and consequent damage. The court is not bound to accept the plaintiff's account merely because it is uncontroved, and where the plaintiff's evidence is inconsistent or is contradicted by contemporaneous medical records, negligence may not be found. The position is modified where the injury is of a kind that does not occur in the absence of negligence and the hospital alone has access to the explanation, in which case res ipsa loquitur shifts the burden onto the hospital to rebut the inference.

citation: Contributory negligence in medical negligence
title: Apportionment where the patient contributed to the injury
content: Where the plaintiff's own conduct contributed to the injury, the plaintiff's negligence may be taken into account and the damages apportioned accordingly. Examples include a patient who continued to use a medication contrary to instructions, refused an essential operation or investigation, failed to attend follow-up appointments, or continued to smoke or drink against medical advice. The principle applies where the plaintiff's conduct falls within the range of ordinary foreseeable conduct and is not so irrational as to break the chain of causation. In a consumer complaint, contributory negligence is treated as a factor in fixing the quantum of compensation rather than as a complete bar to the claim.

citation: Novus actus interveniens
title: Breaking the chain of causation by intervening act
content: Where the injury is so remote from the original negligent act, or is attributable to an intervening act of the plaintiff or of a third party that could not reasonably have been anticipated, the chain of causation is broken and the defendant is not liable in respect of the intervening consequences. The test is whether the intervening act was a natural and probable consequence of the original negligence. In medical negligence it is commonly relied upon where a patient declines or discontinues treatment that was necessary to avert the harm, where a patient obtains care from a second institution that mishandles the case, or where an injury results from an unrelated pre-existing condition that would have manifested itself irrespective of the alleged negligence.

citation: Pre-existing condition and the thin skull rule
title: Pre-existing condition and the thin skull rule
content: The thin skull rule, long recognised in Indian tort law, provides that a defendant must take the plaintiff as they find them. Where a patient suffers from a pre-existing condition such as diabetes, hypertension or an underlying cardiac disorder, and that condition aggravates the injury caused by the defendant's negligence, the defendant is liable for the full extent of the resulting harm even though a healthier patient would not have suffered so severely. The burden of proving that the harm would have occurred in the absence of negligence lies on the defendant. A defendant who contends that the condition was wholly responsible must positively establish that proposition on the evidence, and cannot rest on the mere absence of proof of causation by the plaintiff.

citation: Causation and remoteness of damage
title: Causation in medical negligence — the need for connecting evidence
content: A plaintiff must prove not only that the defendant was negligent but that the negligence caused the injury complained of. Causation is often the hardest element to establish in medical negligence, because the plaintiff's condition may have been deteriorating independently. The plaintiff must ordinarily produce expert medical evidence connecting the alleged act or omission to the resulting harm, or must rely on res ipsa loquitur where the circumstances permit it. A mere temporal sequence, in which the harm followed the treatment, is not by itself sufficient. Where the evidence leaves the question evenly balanced, the claim fails, and the courts do not shift the burden onto the hospital to displace the plaintiff's case by a preponderance of probabilities.

citation: Standard of care — the reasonably competent practitioner
title: The reasonable practitioner standard
content: The standard of care is that of the average reasonably competent practitioner of the same qualification and experience, acting in the same circumstances and at the same time. The standard is objective, not subjective: a defendant cannot escape liability by arguing that the particular conduct adopted was honestly believed to be adequate. The standard is fixed by evidence of what other practitioners in the same position actually do, subject to the Bolam qualification that the practice must be rational and not so divorced from patient safety as to be negligent in itself. In claims against a government or public hospital the standard is the same as in the private sector, though the availability of resources is relevant to what could reasonably have been expected of the institution.

citation: Computation of the two-year limitation period
title: Computing limitation and its commencement
content: The limitation period under section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 runs from the date on which the cause of action arises, which is ordinarily the date of the negligent act or omission, and not the date on which the injury becomes apparent or the date of death. Where the negligence consists of a series of acts, the cause of action arises from the last or the most decisive of them. Where the injury is latent and the plaintiff could not reasonably have known of it, the argument may be advanced that limitation runs from the date of knowledge, but such arguments are construed strictly and the plaintiff should plead the date of knowledge precisely. The prudent practice for a solicitor is to compute the deadline from the date of the incident and file well before the two-year period expires.

citation: Selection of forum for a medical negligence complaint
title: Choosing between District, State and National Commission
content: The forum is determined by the value of the relief claimed. A claim not exceeding fifty lakh rupees lies to the District Commission, a claim exceeding fifty lakh rupees but not exceeding two crore rupees lies to the State Commission, and a claim exceeding two crore rupees lies to the National Commission. The venue is ordinarily where the opposite party resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises. Because a claim for death or permanent disability in a medical negligence matter readily exceeds fifty lakh rupees, such claims are ordinarily instituted before the State Commission or the National Commission, and the State Commission sits in more than one bench across the country, which affects the choice of venue.

citation: Document checklist for a medical negligence complaint
title: Evidence to be assembled for a negligence complaint
content: A medical negligence complaint is won or lost on documents. The essential set comprises the discharge summary, the case sheets and progress notes, the prescription charts and medication administration records, laboratory and radiology reports including images and films, operation notes and anaesthesia records, the referral and transfer records, the consent form actually signed, the itemised bills and payment receipts, and any written correspondence with the hospital. Where injury has occurred, disability and medical assessment certificates from an independent medical officer are required. The plaintiff should also obtain certified copies of the hospital records under an order of the consumer commission where the hospital has failed to disclose them, and should preserve all original files, since the hospital's own records are frequently the best evidence against it.

citation: Pre-litigation expert screening under D'Souza guidelines
title: Obtaining expert opinions before instituting proceedings
content: Before instituting criminal proceedings for medical negligence, the guidelines laid down in Martin F. D'Souza v. Mohd. Ishfaq require the police to obtain an expert opinion from a government or recognised medical college, to give the doctor an opportunity to obtain a counter opinion, and to have a third independent expert resolve the difference. The complaint proceeds only if all three concur. The practical consequence for a plaintiff is that the opinion of an independent medical expert of standing is a precondition to the registration of the complaint, and it is worth obtaining that opinion before approaching the police, not merely afterwards. The guidelines also apply mutatis mutandis to the assessment of civil and consumer claims, where an expert report supporting the allegation of negligence is effectively indispensable.

citation: Effect of institution of proceedings on limitation
title: Whether filing elsewhere stops the limitation clock
content: Sections 12 and 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 exclude from the period of limitation the time during which the plaintiff was prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding against the same party, whether in a competent court or one incapable of jurisdiction. Where a plaintiff institutes a criminal case or a writ against the hospital, and the writ is dismissed for want of maintainability, the defendant may still argue that section 14 has not been satisfied, because the section requires bona fide pursuit of the remedy. Because the two-year period under section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is short, the safe course is to file the complaint within the forum having jurisdiction rather than to rely on exclusion of time spent in an unsuitable proceeding.

citation: Obtaining medical records from a hospital
title: Right to medical records and consequences of refusal
content: A patient is entitled to a copy of his or her medical records, and confidentiality under Article 22A of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 does not defeat the patient's own entitlement to disclosure. Where the hospital refuses, the patient may apply to the consumer commission for a direction to produce the records, or may invoke the freedom of information regime where applicable. The Supreme Court has treated a public hospital as a public authority for that purpose. Failure or refusal to disclose records can be deployed against the hospital at trial, since the burden shifts towards explaining an adverse inference, and in an extreme case the refusal to disclose has itself been treated as an independent and actionable instance of negligence in the delivery of service.

citation: Interim relief in medical negligence proceedings
title: Interim relief available during the pendency of a complaint
content: Section 35(4) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 permits the commission to pass interim orders in a pending complaint where the facts of the case admit of clear-cut issues and to preserve and protect the parties' interests. In medical negligence matters the interim orders most commonly sought are directions for appointment of an independent medical expert to examine the patient and to opine on the standard of care, directions for inspection and production of hospital records, directions to preserve the medical records against destruction or alteration, and orders for deposit of the medical expenses to enable the plaintiff to obtain corrective treatment. Such relief is available from the District Commission as well as from the higher commissions, and is ordinarily granted where the claim discloses prima facie merit.

citation: Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct) Regulations, 2002
title: Professional duties of a medical practitioner
content: The Indian Medical Council's Professional Conduct Regulations prescribe the duties of a medical practitioner in relation to patients. A practitioner is bound to maintain a standard of care and to provide treatment in accordance with accepted medical practice, to keep accurate and confidential patient records, to obtain consent for any procedure, to disclose honestly the nature of a condition and the risks of proposed treatment, to refrain from claiming guarantees of cure, to maintain proper decorum in the professional relationship with the patient, and not to advertise in a manner that denigrates the medical profession. Breach of these obligations, though not of itself a cause of action, is relied upon by the courts as evidence of the standard expected of the profession and of negligence in the particular case. These Regulations have since been superseded by the NMC Medical Professional Conduct Regulations, 2023.

citation: NMC Medical Professional Conduct Regulations, 2023
title: Contemporary medical professional conduct regulations
content: The National Medical Commission Medical Professional Conduct Regulations, 2023 regulate the professional conduct of medical practitioners registered with the Commission. The Regulations consolidate and replace the earlier Indian Medical Council regulations and continue to require a practitioner to provide care consistent with recognised professional standards, to maintain confidentiality, to obtain valid informed consent, to prescribe rationally and to keep records, to avoid misleading claims about cure, and to place the interests of the patient above personal commercial gain. Since the Regulations are recent, reported decisions applying them are still accumulating, and litigation in the interim continues to rely on the settled principles of the older regulations together with the general principles of medical negligence.

citation: Consent and record retention in clinical practice
title: Validity of consent and the duty to retain records
content: A valid consent to treatment must be free, informed, specific and in writing for any invasive procedure, and must correspond to the procedure actually performed. A blanket signature taken on admission does not constitute consent to a particular operation. The duty to maintain records is a professional and legal duty: records ought to be retained for the period prescribed under the applicable medical council regulation, and in any event for a period sufficient to cover the limitation period of the claim, which is two years under section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and three years under section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Destruction, alteration or failure to create records within the period when a claim arises is itself a breach of the standard of care and entitles the court to draw an adverse inference.

citation: Ethical limits on advertising and referral fees
title: Prohibition on fee splitting and misleading advertising
content: The medical professional conduct regulations prohibit a practitioner from advertising treatment in a misleading manner, from claiming guaranteed results, from using testimonials or case studies that amount to advertising, and from splitting fees with a referring practitioner or institution. Fee splitting is associated with the inducement of referrals and the treatment of patients as a means of profit rather than of care. Where a plaintiff can establish that a referral was induced by an undisclosed financial arrangement, the independence of the treating decision is called into question and the court may treat the treating practitioner's judgment as affected by a conflict of interest, which may in turn support an inference of negligence in the treatment that followed.

citation: Duties of nursing and paramedical staff
title: Scope of the duty owed by nursing and ancillary staff
content: Nurses and paramedical staff owe a duty of care to the patient in their own right, and the hospital is additionally vicariously liable for their acts. The duty extends to the correct administration of medication as prescribed and in the prescribed manner, to the monitoring and recording of vital signs, to the timely escalation of deterioration to the treating physician, to the maintenance of infection control and aseptic technique, to the verification and functioning of medical equipment, and to the accurate maintenance of records. A medication error by nursing staff, a failure to escalate a deteriorating patient, or a failure to detect a complication at the bedside is actionable against the hospital as well as against the individual concerned.

citation: Standard of care in emergency and triage situations
title: Standard of care in an emergency
content: Where a patient presents in an emergency, the standard of care is that of a reasonably competent practitioner dealing with that emergency, and the test does not allow the practitioner to take advantage of the impossibility of ideal conditions. A hospital admitting a patient has a duty to assess, stabilise and treat that patient, to conduct the investigations necessary to exclude a life-threatening condition, and to refer to a higher centre where it lacks the facility. In the emergency setting the Bolam qualification is applied with greater latitude to the method of treatment chosen, but not to a failure to attend, to a failure to stabilise, or to a failure to call for senior help when the clinical picture deteriorates. Claims turning on a refusal of admission or on inordinate delay in an emergency are among the most successful categories of medical negligence claim.

citation: Negligence in diagnosis
title: Diagnostic negligence — the standard applied to a missed or wrong diagnosis
content: A claim of diagnostic negligence does not succeed merely by showing that a different diagnosis would have been made. The plaintiff must establish that the defendant failed to reasonably investigate the presenting symptoms, that a reasonably competent practitioner would have reached a different or earlier diagnosis, and that had the correct diagnosis been made earlier the injury complained of would in all probability have been avoided. Because the question is one of probability, it is almost always necessary for the plaintiff to produce expert medical evidence both on the standard of care and on causation, since the countervailing question of whether the plaintiff would have survived in any event is invariably raised by the defendant. Where the symptoms were atypical, or the patient's own account delayed presentation, the defence is correspondingly stronger.

citation: Failure to warn and duty of disclosure
title: The separate duty to warn of risks
content: Beyond the duty to obtain consent, the practitioner bears a duty to warn the patient of such risks attaching to the proposed treatment as are material to a reasonable patient's decision. Materiality is judged by the significance of the risk to the particular patient rather than merely by the frequency of its occurrence, and a risk known to be insignificant to the medical profession may still be material if the patient would have declined the treatment had he known of it. A patient who would not have undertaken the treatment had the risk been properly disclosed has established causation readily, and this is one of the strongest heads of claim arising out of the failure to disclose rare but serious risks such as those associated with a particular drug or implant.

citation: Expert medical evidence in negligence claims
title: The necessity and role of expert evidence
content: In a medical negligence claim the court is assisted by, and in practice almost always requires, the opinion of a medical expert. The expert must be of the same qualification and experience as the defendant in the relevant discipline, must be independent, and must examine the plaintiff where an examination is required. The expert is expected to address each of the four essential questions: whether the defendant owed a duty of care, whether there was a breach of that duty measured against the accepted standard, whether the breach caused the injury, and what the consequences of the injury are. A claim that proceeds without supporting expert evidence is very unlikely to succeed, whatever the apparent merits, and the Court's own medical adviser assists the judge but does not replace the plaintiff's burden of proof.

citation: Consumer Commissions — practice note on proof of quantum
title: Proving the amount claimed in a compensation claim
content: The complainant must ordinarily produce documentary support for the heads of compensation claimed, namely the medical expenditure, the receipts for the treatment, the cost of travel and attendant, and evidence of the loss of income. Where the loss of income cannot be supported by salary records, particularly in the case of a self-employed or daily-wage patient, the commission may accept testimony corroborated by a certificate from the employer or an income-tax return, and may decline a claim that rests entirely on an unparticularised assertion. Following Ramashankar Prasad v. Dr. Amod Kumar, a rigid insistence on documentary proof of every item is not required, but a contemporaneous, itemised and plausible account of the expenditure is expected, and unexplained lump-sum claims are routinely reduced.
